name: Accessible first
summary: Large text, large targets and AAA contrast for the text you must read, so everyone can finish the task.
description: Accessible first is an Open DS scheme: a full set of answers to the Open DS grammar, with the reasons behind each, usage rules, voice and tone, and the tokens that follow. Large text, large targets and AAA contrast for the text you must read, so everyone can finish the task.

ai.use_when: Public services, health, government and any product that must work for everyone.
ai.avoid_when: Dense expert tools where screen space matters more than size.

Resizing means dragging panels in desktop tools. The scheme avoids widgets that need drag or precise pointing, and avoids dense expert tools.
A component joins only when it works with any assistive technology. The native select covers the same choice and every assistive technology understands it.
Only dialogs separate from the page here, with a dimmed page and a border. A panel sliding in from an edge adds a layer the scheme does not use.
Sidebar is for apps people move around all session. Here people do this once or twice a year, and breadcrumb shows where they are.
Spinner already says the page is working. Accessible first keeps one clear way to do each thing, so a second loading state is not added.
The scheme avoids widgets that need drag or precise pointing. A person with a tremor completes a form here, and an exact answer is typed.
Components do their work in forms and steps, where a choice waits for the form. The catalogue gives that case to the checkbox.
A toast goes away. Here errors and important notes stay on the page, because people must know what went wrong and where.
Icons never stand alone here, so no control needs a hover hint. Touch screens never hover, and optional help sits in a section a person can open.

default.label: Accessible first
default.description: The single brand: strong blue on true neutral, high contrast everywhere.

theme.$description: The Accessible first theme: what each brand-dependent semantic key picks, in light and dark, plus mode-free picks (fonts, corners) in base. Info uses teal, kept apart from the brand color so it never reads as an action. Categories 1 to 5 are blue, teal, green, amber, gray: distinct hues for tags and chart series, with no meaning. Disabled uses the neutral gray.

open-ds.why: radius.6: We use a 6px corner for buttons and inputs in order to mark their role as controls in a calm, clear tone, by brand convention. A slight radius does this by softening the edge while the box keeps a clear rectangle. So every field and button reads plainly as something to use, because the brand is calm and clear (brand.q1) and corners are slightly rounded (shape.values).

radius.4: We use a 4px corner for badges and checkboxes in order to give marks a role of their own, apart from the 6px controls. We use 24px for the inline padding inside controls in order to give content room inside its box: three base steps (3 × 8px), the same as a card's padding. Padding does this by keeping content off the edge of its box, so the content reads as part of that box, and by setting the size of the box with the content. So each button is a bigger target that is easy to hit, because everyone uses it, including people with motor needs (people.q1), and the smallest target is large (accessibility.values).

We use 24px for the padding inside cards and dialogs in order to give content room inside its box: three base steps (3 × 8px), half again the default gap. Padding does this by the rule given for space.inset.control-x, so content stays clear of the strong border at any zoom, because everyone uses it (people.q1) and each step must take low effort to understand (human.q1).

We use 16px for the inline padding inside table cells in order to give content room inside its box: two base steps (2 × 8px), the same as the default gap. Padding does this by the rule given for space.inset.control-x, so values in two columns stay apart at high zoom, because everyone uses it, including people with low vision (people.q1), and the layout is spacious (spacing.values).

A large target sets the 52px default. The step is 4px, so compact stays at the 48px large target size; large equals the default, as every control is already large. Rows are a decision of their own and stay one control tall.

default.$description: Height of buttons and inputs, and the smallest target.

open-ds.why: We use 52px for buttons and inputs in order to make a hit target: the large target size, step 0 of the control scale, a 52px hit area above the 44px of WCAG 2.5.5. Height does this by setting the hit area a finger or a pointer must hit; WCAG measures the hit area, not the drawn box (2.5.8: 24px at AA; 2.5.5: 44px at AAA), and padding or a label can make it larger than the box. So people with tremor and low vision get a large control, because the smallest target is large (accessibility.values) and everyone uses it, including people with motor needs (people.q1).

We use 48px for compact controls, such as a button inside a field, in order to make a hit target: one 4px step below the 52px default on the control scale, a short step so the 48px hit area still meets the large target size. Height does this by the rule given for size.control.default, so a button fits inside a field and is still large, because the smallest target is large (accessibility.values) and everyone uses it (people.q1).

large.$description: Height of large controls. Not used in this system, so it equals the default.

open-ds.why: We use 52px for large controls in order to make a hit target: the default's step on the control scale and the default's 52px hit area, as every control is already large and the scheme has no hero action. Height does this by the rule given for size.control.default, so every button has one height and pages stay predictable, because each step must take low effort to understand (human.q1) and the smallest target is large (accessibility.values).

We use 52px for one table row in order to keep the eye on its row: a row is one 52px default control tall, as rows stay one control tall. Row height does this by making each row a band the eye follows across, and a hit target when the row is clickable (WCAG 2.5.8: 24px). So rows are easy to read and tap, and a control sits in a row with no gap, because row heights are a spacing role, for touch and zoom (spacing.roles), and the smallest target is large (accessibility.values).
One icon size, 20px, one step larger than the 19px body text it sits beside, so every icon stays easy to see.

hit-area.$description: The least hit area of a control. A control drawn smaller keeps its size; its hit area grows past it, never into a neighbour.

open-ds.why: We use a 44px hit area for controls drawn smaller, such as a checkbox, a radio or a switch, in order to make a hit target a fingertip can find: the WCAG 2.5.5 size. The hit area does this by growing past the drawn box through a pseudo-element, and rows in a group stand at least 44px apart, so no two targets overlap. So people tap the right control on a phone, because targets are sized for large, easy hits (accessibility.values) and the layout leaves room for it (spacing.values).

open-ds.why: We use a fixed 2px focus offset in order to keep focus visible by contrast, not for style. The gap does this by showing the page color between ring and control, so one of the two colors keeps enough contrast against any fill (W3C technique C40). So people see the ring on any fill and at any zoom, because every state has its own look (accessibility.roles).

Few sizes: a large 19px body and a 1.22 ratio, each role on the next step, and no step under 16px. Headings sit tight at 1.25; every other role wraps at 1.6, labels too, because a label wraps when people zoom.

Display is 36px, three ratio steps above the 19px body (19 × 1.22^3 = 34.5), snapped up to the 4px grid as headings are, kept off page titles: it changes from page to page and pushes the content down.
Display lines are 1.25 times its 36px size, 45px; as a ratio, the line height grows with the text when people zoom.
Display is bold, 700, one of the two weights the scheme loads; bold and the 36px size together mark the top of the page.
Title is 28px, two ratio steps above body and one clear step under display, the same on every page, so people always know where they are.
Title lines are 1.25 times its 28px size, 35px, the same tight ratio as display, and they grow with the text on zoom.
Title is bold, 700, so the 28px page title reads as a heading and never as large body text.
Heading is 24px, one ratio step above the 19px body (23.2px) snapped up to the 4px grid, and one under the 28px title, so a section inside a form step stands out.
Heading lines are 1.25 times its 24px size, 30px: the smallest role on the tight ratio, while text from 19px down takes 1.6.
Heading is bold, 700: at 24px it sits only one ratio step above body, so weight, not size alone, sets it apart.
Body is 19px, step 0 of the scale and one ratio step above the 16px caption, because large text is readable for more people.
Body lines are 1.6 times its 19px size, 30.4px: the open ratio for paragraphs, so short lines of large text lower effort.
Body is regular, 400, the plain weight for paragraphs; bold stays for the roles that mark structure.
Label shares step 0 with body at 19px, because form labels and hints are where type matters most; weight, not size, sets it apart.
Label lines are 1.6 times its 19px size, 30.4px, so a label that wraps above its field keeps the open spacing of body.
Label is bold, 700: at 19px it shares the body size, so bold marks it as the field's always visible label.
Caption is one ratio step under body (19 ÷ 1.22), 16px, exactly 1rem: even secondary text never drops below the reader's own default size.
Caption lines are 1.6 times its 16px size, 25.6px: the smallest text keeps the open ratio and grows with the text on zoom.
Caption is regular, 400, not bold: it carries secondary text, and the scheme loads only regular and bold.
Data shares step 0 with body at 19px, not a small or mono size, because every number must be readable at large size.
Data lines match body, 1.6 times 19px, 30.4px, so numbers in a table read with the same room as text.
Data is regular, 400, like body, so numbers in a table read as plain content and not as labels.

feedback.$description: Hover, press and toggle feedback. At most 150ms in a productive family.

open-ds.why: We use 150ms (moderate) for hover, press and toggle feedback in order to confirm each action inside the productive limit of 150ms. The duration does this by ending the change before the eye leaves the control. So people see each action land and never wait for it, because motion is for feedback only, which makes the family productive (motion.roles), and feedback feels moderate (motion.values).

panels.$description: Menus, popovers, dialogs and drawers opening. At most 300ms in a productive family.

open-ds.why: We use 150ms (moderate) for menus, popovers, dialogs and other panels in order to show where a panel comes from, inside the productive limit of 300ms. The duration does this by giving the eye just enough frames to follow the panel from its trigger. So people see where a panel came from and keep their place, because the family is productive (motion.roles) and there is one speed (motion.count).

exit.$description: A layer closing. About 150ms, never more, in a productive family.

open-ds.why: We use the feedback duration, 150ms (moderate), for a layer that closes in order to finish the exit move within the productive 150ms. The duration does this by removing the layer in fewer frames than an open takes, as nothing in it needs reading any more. So people get the page back at once, because productive exits stay short (motion.roles) and there is one speed (motion.count).

standard.$description: The transition move: a state that changes in place, such as hover, press or toggle.

open-ds.why: We use the standard easing (0.2, 0, 0, 1) for state changes in place in order to do the transition move. The curve does this by reaching its target early and settling slowly, with no overshoot. So a hover, a press or a toggle lands at once and then stays still, because easing is a standard ease-out (motion.definition) and the family is productive (motion.roles).

enter.$description: The enter move: a layer that appears.

open-ds.why: We use the transition move's standard easing for a panel that appears in order to do the enter move. The curve does this by spending most of the change in the first frames, so the layer is in place before it slows. So people can read a menu almost as soon as it opens, because easing is a standard ease-out (motion.definition) in a productive family (motion.roles).

exit.$description: The exit move: a layer that closes in place.

open-ds.why: We use the strong-out easing (0.23, 1, 0.32, 1) for a layer that closes in place in order to do the exit move of the productive family. The curve does this by covering most of the way in the first third of its time, then easing to a stop. So a closed popover is gone before the next click, because productive exits take a strong ease-out (motion.roles) and easing never springs here (motion.definition).

exit-offscreen.$description: The exit move of a layer that slides off the screen: a sheet or a drawer.

open-ds.why: We use the exit move's strong-out easing for a drawer or sheet that slides off the screen, in order to keep every exit of a productive family on one fast curve. The curve does this by moving fastest at the start, so the panel clears the view with no slow tail. So the content under a closing sheet comes back at once, because only an expressive family accelerates what leaves the screen (motion.roles), and easing is a plain ease-out (motion.definition).

emphasize.$description: The emphasize move: a moment that calls for attention.

open-ds.why: We use the transition move's standard easing for a moment that calls for attention in order to give the emphasize move no overshoot. The curve does this by stopping at its target without passing it. So a new message draws the eye by its change, not by a bounce, because the family is productive (motion.roles) and easing is a standard ease-out, never a spring (motion.definition).
